# The First Seven Years

> Expert answers for parents of children aged 0–7, from the podcast and video series hosted by Dr. Murray Clarke with co-host Bryce Wylde. Educational content, not medical advice. Each answer names the expert, shows publish and review dates, and links to the source video.

## Parent answers
- [Is my child’s eczema really a gut problem?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/is-my-childs-eczema-a-gut-problem/): Partly — and it is worth knowing why. Eczema happens when the skin barrier is leaky and the immune system over-reacts. Research increasingly links both to the gut microbiome, especially in the first years of life. Good skin care still comes first; supporting the gut can sit alongside it.
- [What is “leaky gut”, really?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/what-is-leaky-gut/): “Leaky gut” describes a gut lining that lets more through than it should — researchers call it increased intestinal permeability. It is measurable in studies, but it is not a diagnosis on its own. Think of it as one way gut health may connect to allergies, skin and mood.
- [Prebiotics, probiotics, postbiotics — what’s the difference?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/prebiotics-vs-probiotics-vs-postbiotics/): Probiotics are live, helpful microbes. Prebiotics are the fibres that feed them. Postbiotics are the useful compounds those microbes make. For most children, foods are the easiest place to start: yogurt or kefir, oats, bananas, beans and a wide variety of plants.
- [How do I help my child’s gut recover after antibiotics?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/restoring-the-gut-after-antibiotics/): First, antibiotics are sometimes essential — always finish the course you were prescribed. Afterwards, a varied, fibre-rich diet, fermented foods if tolerated, plenty of water and time all help the microbiome rebuild. Ask your pediatrician whether a probiotic is worth adding for your child.
- [Are pets and a bit of dirt actually good for my child?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/are-pets-and-dirt-good-for-immunity/): Often, yes. Many studies link early, everyday exposure — pets, outdoor play, older siblings — to lower rates of allergy and asthma. It is sometimes called the “old friends” idea. It does not replace handwashing before meals and after the toilet.
- [Is it okay to kiss my baby on the face?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/is-it-okay-to-kiss-my-baby/): For healthy parents, affectionate contact is part of normal bonding and shares friendly microbes. The exceptions: if you have a cold sore, a cold or flu, or your newborn is very young or unwell, keep kisses away from the face and hands until you are better.
- [Can stress in pregnancy affect my baby?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/can-stress-in-pregnancy-affect-my-baby/): Research links ongoing, severe stress in pregnancy with differences in a baby’s development — but everyday worry is normal and nothing to feel guilty about. Sleep, support, gentle movement and asking for help are protective for both of you.
- [Does my own gut health before pregnancy matter?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/does-my-gut-health-before-pregnancy-matter/): It is part of the story. Babies pick up their first microbes from their mother — through birth, feeding and close contact. Eating a varied, fibre-rich diet and looking after your own health before and during pregnancy all count.
- [Why are ADHD diagnoses rising?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/why-are-adhd-diagnoses-rising/): Partly because awareness and screening have improved. Researchers are also looking at sleep, screens, diet and the gut–brain axis. In this clip, Dr. Dan Sullivan shares his view on what has changed — and what parents can do day to day.
- [What should my baby’s first food be?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/what-should-my-babys-first-food-be/): There is no single perfect first food. Around six months, many pediatricians suggest offering a variety of iron-rich, soft foods — such as well-cooked meat or fish, beans and lentils, or an iron-fortified cereal — rather than relying on one bland cereal. In this video, Dr. Bill Sears explains why he looks beyond rice cereal. Ask your pediatrician about timing, allergens and safe textures.
- [Is cortisone cream okay for my baby’s eczema?](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/answers/is-cortisone-cream-safe-for-babies/): Low-strength steroid creams are widely prescribed and can be appropriate for short flares. In this clip, Joy McCarthy explains why she also looks at gentle skin care and gut support. Talk to your pediatrician before stopping or changing anything prescribed.

## Topics
- [Gut health & microbiome](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/gut-health/): Much of your child’s immune system lives in the gut, and the microbes that settle there in the first years shape far more than digestion. Start here for the plain-English basics.
- [Nutrition & first foods](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/first-foods/): From first spoonfuls to lunchbox years — how to build a varied diet without turning mealtimes into a project.
- [Picky eating](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/picky-eating/): Selective eating is one of the most common worries we hear. What is normal, what helps, and when to look closer.
- [Skin & eczema](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/skin-eczema/): Eczema is about more than skin. Our experts explain barrier care, triggers, and where the gut fits in.
- [Allergies](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/allergies/): What research now says about early exposure, and how to tell an allergy from an intolerance.
- [Immunity & everyday illness](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/immunity/): Coughs, colds and the endless nursery bugs — building resilience, and knowing when to call the doctor.
- [Brain, focus & ADHD](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/brain-focus/): Why attention differences are being diagnosed more often, and the daily habits that support a developing brain.
- [Autism & development](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/autism-development/): Understanding developmental differences early, and the range of support families are exploring.
- [Sleep](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/sleep/): Sleep drives mood, growth and immunity. Gentle, realistic approaches for tired families.
- [Emotions & behaviour](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/emotions/): Meltdowns are normal — here is what is happening in the brain, and how to help a child find calm.
- [Pregnancy & preconception](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/pregnancy/): A child’s health story starts before birth. What matters in preconception and pregnancy — without the guilt.
- [Supplements](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/supplements/): Food first — then an honest look at where vitamin D, omega-3s, probiotics and others may fit.
- [Omega-3s & healthy fats](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/topics/omega-3s/): Fats are a building material for a young child’s brain and eyes. What omega-3s are, where to find them in everyday food, and what to ask before adding anything extra.

## Experts
- [Dr. Murray Clarke](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/experts/dr-murray-clarke/): Host of The First Seven Years and the doctor who answers your questions.
- [Dr. Bill Sears](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/experts/dr-bill-sears/): Pediatrician and author of more than 40 books on parenting and children’s health, including The Baby Book.
- [Bryce Wylde](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/experts/bryce-wylde/): Co-host, functional medicine expert, and author of The First Seven Years book.
- [Dr. Dan Sullivan](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/experts/dr-dan-sullivan/): Guest on Episode 27 — ADHD, stress and the gut.
- [Dr. Elisa Song](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/experts/dr-elisa-song/): Integrative pediatrician; guest on Episode 26 — the gut behind allergies, anxiety and ADHD.
- [Joy McCarthy](https://thefirstsevenyears.com/experts/joy-mccarthy/): Holistic nutritionist; guest on eczema and the gut–skin connection.
